label: Weinstein's Lagrangian Neighborhood
notes: Open by framing the question for printed pages 49 through 54: how much of the symplectic geometry near a Lagrangian is determined by the Lagrangian alone. The answer is essentially all of it. A tubular neighborhood is symplectomorphic to a neighborhood of the zero section in the cotangent bundle, so the germ depends only on the diffeomorphism type of the base.

label: The Linear Observation
notes: Stress that the whole theorem rests on one piece of linear algebra. When a subspace is Lagrangian, the symplectic form gives a nondegenerate pairing between the quotient and the subspace itself. That pairing identifies the quotient with the dual space. Verify with students that adding a vector inside the Lagrangian leaves the pairing unchanged, so it descends to the quotient cleanly.

label: Normal Bundle Equals Cotangent
notes: Globalize the linear fact fiber by fiber. The symplectic form trivializes the symplectic orthogonal, so the normal bundle of a Lagrangian is canonically the cotangent bundle of that Lagrangian. This is the model space the theorem will match. Emphasize canonical: no choice of metric or complement is needed, the identification comes straight from omega.

label: The Cotangent Model
notes: Recall the tautological and canonical forms on the cotangent bundle so the model side is concrete. The zero section is Lagrangian, and its neighborhood carries the standard form. Students should leave this slide knowing exactly what they are mapping into: a neighborhood of the zero section equipped with minus d of the tautological one-form.

label: Statement of the Theorem
notes: State the Weinstein Lagrangian neighborhood theorem precisely. Given a Lagrangian in any symplectic manifold, there is a symplectomorphism from a neighborhood of it onto a neighborhood of the zero section that restricts to the identity on the Lagrangian. Underline that this upgrades the ordinary tubular neighborhood theorem by preserving the symplectic form, not just the smooth structure.

label: Proof via Relative Moser
notes: Walk through the proof architecture. Build two forms agreeing on the Lagrangian using the cotangent model, then interpolate. The relative Moser theorem produces an isotopy fixing the Lagrangian and carrying one form to the other. Highlight that agreement along the submanifold, plus matching on the conormal directions, is exactly what relative Moser needs to start.

label: Nearby Lagrangians as One-Forms
notes: Now harvest the payoff. Inside the cotangent model, a section is a one-form on the base, and its graph is a submanifold. A short computation with the tautological form shows the graph is Lagrangian precisely when the one-form is closed. So Lagrangians near the zero section correspond exactly to closed one-forms on the base.

label: Intersections Are Zeros
notes: Connect geometry to analysis. A nearby Lagrangian meets the zero section exactly where its defining one-form vanishes. When the first de Rham cohomology vanishes, closed forms are exact, so the form is the differential of a function and intersection points are critical points of that function. Morse theory then bounds the number of intersections from below.

label: Graphs Near the Diagonal
notes: Apply the same machinery to symplectomorphisms. In the product with the twisted form, the diagonal is Lagrangian and so is the graph of any symplectomorphism. A graph close to the diagonal becomes a one-form near the zero section, closed exactly when the map is symplectic. Fixed points are where the graph meets the diagonal, hence zeros of the form.

label: The Lagrangian Creed
notes: Articulate Weinstein's creed: everything is a Lagrangian submanifold. Symplectomorphisms, fixed-point problems, and generating functions all become statements about Lagrangians and their intersections. This reframing is the organizing philosophy behind much of the field and motivates the constructions of the following lectures.

label: Toward Arnold and Floer
notes: Close by pointing forward. The near-identity fixed-point count generalizes: Arnold conjectured that a Hamiltonian time-one map has at least as many fixed points as a function on the manifold has critical points, with period-one orbits playing the role of intersections. Floer homology makes this rigorous. Recap the chain from the linear pairing to these global bounds.
